posts.text:
Happy Veterans Day to the brave men and women who have fought for and protected the greatest nation in the world. 

We are forever grateful for your service and sacrifice. https://t.co/zuQJthh9YR

Hurricane Isaias is expected to make its way through Georgia this weekend. 

Please be sure to monitor local weather alerts and follow tips from @GeorgiaEMAHS to prepare. Stay safe. https://t.co/U9DoYuUTd6

Please join Leigh Ann and me in prayer for the loved ones of Captain Tim Tallant, who has unexpectedly passed away. Captain Tallant was a longtime public servant and cherished member of the Walton County Sheriff’s Office who is being remembered by colleagues as a man of character who made a difference in the lives of those who knew him.

Proud to have led to the Water Resources Development Act, which passed the House of Representatives this evening.

From the Ports of Savannah and Brunswick to locks, dams, and waterways across the nation, the state of Georgia and all America depend on reliable water infrastructure. 

WRDA 2026 cuts red tape, speeds up project delivery, and empowers the Army Corps of Engineers to execute its mission while holding it accountable to keep projects on schedule and on budget.

Proud to work with @USACEHQ to help secure $12M to complete the nourishment project for Tybee Island.

This investment is critical to restoring the shoreline, strengthening protection for homes and businesses ahead of future storms, and preserving the beach that receives over 1 million visitors annually. 

Great win for Coastal Georgia!

It was an honor to welcome Phillip Martin and Patsey Schreiber from the Veterans of Foreign Wars Department of Georgia to the office today to discuss how Congress can better serve our veterans.

It’s time to PASS the Major Richard Star Act! https://t.co/NuQ3axKJqK

It was great to welcome @DrOzCMS to the 10th District to meet with local leaders and healthcare professionals to discuss the record investment in rural healthcare.

Together, we are supporting rural Georgia and giving patients the opportunity to get the care they deserve, when and where they need it.

September 11, 2001. It’s hard to believe it has been 25 years since that terrible day when we lost thousands of Americans to a terrorist attack that changed the world forever. 

Those old enough to recall that day remember exactly where they were when they heard the news and all the fear, confusion, anger, and pain as our country was under attack.

In the midst of tragedy, we also saw the best of America: First responders and civilians rushing toward danger to save others, many making the ultimate sacrifice. We saw passengers on United Airlines Flight 93 heroically stop the terrorists from inflicting more damage knowing that they could not save themselves. We saw our country rally together in a way rarely seen before and since. 

Today my prayers are with those who all these years later still grieve the loss of loved ones, and for our great country and its future.
Go Dawgs! https://t.co/R7S7BzEPOk

Sec. Telle is a tremendous leader and it has been my privilege to work with him to improve and modernize American water infrastructure.

I know that he will take the same relentless drive to ensuring American soldiers have the tools they need to fight and win. https://t.co/bZ6Aq4risv

Proud to receive the @FaithandFreedom Coalition’s Friend of the Family Award. 

Families are the foundation of American greatness, and I will continue to champion pro-family policies and defend religious liberty as a member of Congress.

Thank you for this honor. https://t.co/vKRetPKlrS

On this day in history in 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his most iconic speech, “I Have a Dream,” to over 250,000 people on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial.

The March on Washington was a peaceful rally advocating for voting rights and an end to discrimination and segregation against African Americans. A year later, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 was enacted, prohibiting discrimination in employment and education and ending segregation in public places.

posts.text:
Great morning with local leaders and businesses at the Gwinnett Chamber Congressional Appreciation Breakfast.

Main Street is the backbone of our communities and the engine of the American economy. Small businesses create jobs, strengthen our communities, and keep Georgia moving forward.
“May the Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; the Lord turn his face toward you and give you peace.” — Numbers 6:24-26

On this day in history in 1940, Leon Trotsky, the exiled Russian revolutionary, was fatally injured by an ice-ax-wielding assassin working for Soviet leader Joseph Stalin, at his home in Mexico. 

Trotsky, born in Ukraine, became a leading Marxist revolutionary and key figure in the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution, later building the Red Army to win the Civil War. His clashes with Stalin led to his exile and eventual expulsion from the Soviet Union.

Thank you to the 140 students and parents who joined us for GA-10’s Academy Day to learn more about our nation’s military service academies and the Congressional Nomination process.

Academy Day gives students interested in serving our country the information, resources, and guidance they need to successfully navigate the application process.

I’m proud to see so many young Georgians ready to answer the call to serve our country!

On this day in history in 1877, the infamous Western outlaw Billy the Kid claimed his first victim after a skirmish with a blacksmith.

Billy the Kid’s real name was likely Henry McCarty, though he was better known by the alias William H. Bonney. His short, violent life was filled with prison breaks and shootouts. The gunslinger claimed to have killed 21 men, “one for every year of my life,” but historians put the true number closer to nine. Billy was shot and killed by New Mexico Sheriff Pat Garrett on July 14, 1881.
“Commit to the Lord whatever you do, and he will establish your plans.” — Proverbs 16:3

On this day in history in 1981, IBM releases its version of a personal computer, or PC. 

IBM CEO Frank Cary gave William Lowe one month to develop a prototype for a PC that appealed to small businesses and consumers for $1,500. He was given a year to take it to market. 

The IBM PC became the industry standard as it was now possible to connect to a television, allowing users to manage text and play games. It improved business efficiency, drove the growth of the software industry, and brought computing into widespread use.

On this day in history in 1934, the nation’s most dangerous criminals arrived at Alcatraz.

Converted into a maximum-security federal penitentiary in 1934, Alcatraz held notorious criminals such as Al Capone, George “Machine Gun” Kelly, and Robert Stroud, the “Birdman of Alcatraz.” The prison became infamous for escape attempts—most notably the 1962 breakout by Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers, which inspired the film Escape from Alcatraz.

Due to high maintenance costs, Alcatraz closed in 1963 after housing over 1,500 inmates in its 29-year run.

On this day in history in 1776, news of America’s Declaration of Independence reached London.

Dispatches from General Howe had finally crossed the Atlantic and arrived by horseback. On August 10, the London Gazette carried a short line confirming that the Continental Congress had declared the United Colonies “free and independent States.” What many in Britain had viewed as a colonial uprising was now an official war.
“Praise the Lord, all you nations; extol him, all you peoples. For great is his love toward us, and the faithfulness of the Lord endures forever. Praise the Lord.” — Psalm 117:1-2

On this day in history in 1782, George Washington created the Purple Heart during his time as the commander in chief of the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War. 

He awarded it to only three soldiers during the Revolutionary War. The purple badge allowed soldiers to pass guards without challenge and have their names recorded in the “Book of Merit.” The award was forgotten until it was reinstated on Washington’s 200th birthday in 1932. 

Today, the Purple Heart is awarded to soldiers who have been wounded, killed, or prisoners of war. It is the oldest American award for the armed forces.

On this day in history in 1945, the United States dropped the first atomic bomb on the city of Hiroshima in Japan.  

The U.S. began developing nuclear weapons in 1940 after learning Germany was doing the same. Although Germany was defeated before the bomb was ready, the war with Japan continued. To avoid heavy U.S. casualties, President Truman ordered the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, killing 80,000 instantly and 60,000 more from fallout. Days later, a second bomb hit Nagasaki. Japan surrendered a week later, ending World War II.

I’m working to help more young Americans achieve the American Dream.

Traditionally, 529 College Savings Plans could only pay for four-year degrees, but we know that’s not the right or necessary path for everyone. That’s why I introduced the bipartisan Aviation Workforce Development Act and then co-authored the Freedom to Invest in Tomorrow’s Workforce Act, which expanded 529s to cover virtually every trade and certification as part of the Working Families Tax Cut.

Now, more people can pursue the path that’s right for them with the same tools as those who want to go to college.

On this day in history in 1926, master illusionist Harry Houdini was submerged underwater in an airtight metal casket after being challenged by rival magician Rahman Bey. It would take Houdini 91 minutes to escape.

This was the final major stunt of a career filled with daring escapes and illusions. Three months later, Houdini died at age 52 from complications of a ruptured appendix. He was laid to rest at Machpelah Cemetery in Queens, New York.
